title: Pneumothorax, blebs and pleurodesis: primary versus secondary, tension decompression and VATS bullectomy
subject: ss-ctvs
refs: Sabiston Textbook of Surgery 22e Ch 57 (Pneumothorax and Pleural Disease)
British Thoracic Society Guideline for Pleural Disease: Spontaneous Pneumothorax

steps.say: Primary spontaneous pneumothorax occurs in young, tall, thin individuals without underlying clinical lung disease. Patients are typically fifteen to thirty-five years of age, with male predominance and strong association with cigarette smoking. Spontaneous rupture of subpleural apical blebs releases air into the pleural space.
steps.tx: A **primary spontaneous pneumothorax** occurs in tall, thin individuals aged 15 to 35 years without overt lung pathology. High negative transpulmonary apical gradients generate high mechanical alveolar stress, precipitating the spontaneous rupture of congenital **apical blebs** or subpleural bullae into the negative intrapleural space.

vis.caption: Chest radiographic signs of visceral pleural line displacement and pneumothorax. Credit: StewardMD.
vis.alt: Chest radiograph showing apical visceral pleural line displacement and absent peripheral lung markings.

steps.say: Secondary spontaneous pneumothorax arises as a complication of underlying parenchymal lung disease. It most frequently complicates chronic obstructive pulmonary disease with emphysema, followed by cystic fibrosis, necrotizing pneumonia, and tuberculosis. Because underlying pulmonary reserve is poor, even a small collapse can cause respiratory failure.
steps.tx: In contrast, a **secondary spontaneous pneumothorax** develops in the presence of established parenchymal lung disease, most commonly advanced **COPD emphysema**, suppurative **cystic fibrosis**, or cavitating necrotizing pneumonia. Impaired baseline pulmonary reserve makes secondary pneumothorax life-threatening even with minimal percentage lung collapse.

left.title: Primary Spontaneous Pneumothorax
points: Aged 15 to 35 years; tall, asthenic body habitus
Normal underlying lung parenchyma with apical blebs
Tolerates moderate collapse with mild tachypnea

right.title: Secondary Spontaneous Pneumothorax
points: Older patients with advanced COPD or cystic fibrosis
Severe underlying destruction of lung architecture
Presents with acute hypercapnic respiratory failure

steps.say: Tension pneumothorax is an acute clinical emergency driven by a one-way valve mechanism. Air enters the pleural space during inspiration but cannot exit during expiration. Intrapleural pressure rises above atmospheric pressure, causing mediastinal shift, compression of the venae cavae, and severe obstructive shock.
steps.tx: A **tension pneumothorax** arises via a one-way flap valve mechanism. Progressive positive intrapleural pressure produces contralateral **mediastinal shift**, kinking of the great veins, decreased venous return, and acute circulatory collapse from profound **obstructive shock**, requiring immediate clinical diagnosis without delaying for chest radiography.

nodes.label: One-way visceral pleural tear traps inspired air in pleural cavity
Intrapleural pressure turns positive, shifting mediastinum to contralateral side
Compression of superior and inferior vena cava abolishes venous return
Immediate obstructive shock and pulseless electrical activity arrest

steps.say: Emergency decompression of tension pneumothorax requires immediate needle thoracostomy. Insert a large-bore fourteen-gauge catheter into the second intercostal space in the midclavicular line, or alternatively in the fourth or fifth space in the anterior axillary line. Convert immediately to tube thoracostomy.
steps.tx: Emergency management mandates immediate **needle thoracostomy** using a large-bore **14-gauge catheter**. The needle is inserted in the **second intercostal space** along the midclavicular line or the 4th/5th intercostal space anterior axillary line, rapidly decompressing trapped pleural gas, followed immediately by formal tube thoracostomy.

rows: 2nd ICS midclavicular or 4th/5th ICS anterior axillary line
Advance 14-gauge cannula over superior rib margin
Rapid pleural entry with blunt finger sweep in ventilated patients
Direct chest tube posteriorly and toward pulmonary apex

steps.say: Surgical intervention is indicated to prevent recurrent collapse. Key indications in primary spontaneous pneumothorax include a second ipsilateral episode, any contralateral episode, synchronous bilateral pneumothorax, or an air leak persisting longer than three to five days. High-risk occupations also mandate definitive surgery.
steps.tx: Standard **surgical indications** in primary pneumothorax encompass a **first recurrence** (second ipsilateral episode), initial contralateral occurrence, bilateral synchronous collapse, or a **persistent air leak** exceeding 3 to 5 days. Surgery is also advised after a single episode in pilots or divers.

nodes.label: Evaluate pneumothorax history, episode count, and occupation
First episode: conservative care or chest tube drainage
Recurrence, air leak > 3-5 days, or high-risk profession

steps.say: Video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery bullectomy is the operative standard. Using endoscopic surgical staplers, the surgeon inspects the lung apex and resects all visible subpleural blebs and bullae. The superior segment of the lower lobe is also inspected, as blebs frequently occur there as well.
steps.tx: Minimally invasive **VATS bullectomy** employs an **endoscopic stapler** to resect subpleural **apical blebs** and bullae under video guidance. Dissection systematically explores both the apex of the upper lobe and the superior segment of the lower lobe, resecting target bullous lesions with healthy margins.

left.title: VATS Bullectomy
points: Endoscopic stapler wedge resection of apical blebs
Significantly lower post-op pain and shorter hospital stay

right.title: Open Axillary Thoracotomy
points: Reserved for dense pleural adhesions or reoperative failure
Marginally lower recurrence rate at cost of incision pain

steps.say: Always combine bullectomy with pleurodesis to induce dense pleural symphysis. Mechanical pleurodesis using Marlex mesh or gauze abrasion, or apical parietal pleurectomy, creates controlled sterile inflammation. This obliteration of the pleural space reduces long-term recurrence rates to under two to five percent.
steps.tx: Wedge resection is combined with **mechanical pleurodesis** (pleural abrasion using dry gauze or mesh) or apical **parietal pleurectomy**. Denuding the mesothelium stimulates intense sterile fibroblastic adhesions between the visceral and parietal pleura, achieving significant **recurrence reduction** to under 2 to 5 percent.

rows: Surgical stripping of apical parietal pleura
Dry gauze or mesh scoring of parietal pleura

steps.say: Chemical pleurodesis is a valuable option in patients who cannot tolerate surgery. Insufflating sterile talc poudrage via thoracoscopy or administering talc slurry through a chest tube triggers intense pleural inflammation. Talc is particularly useful for secondary spontaneous pneumothorax in elderly or debilitated patients.
steps.tx: **Chemical pleurodesis** employing aerosolized **talc poudrage** during thoracoscopy or instillation of **talc slurry** via a chest tube generates intense, diffuse aseptic inflammation. Talc remains the most effective chemical sclerosant, particularly beneficial for secondary pneumothorax in patients unfit for general anesthesia.
